paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: the modern periodic law
paragraphs.meaning: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and found that properties repeated periodically, but a few elements sat in the wrong place until the order was changed to atomic number. The modern periodic law states that properties are a periodic function of atomic number. The long form of the table then follows the filling order of orbitals, which is why the blocks are named after the subshell being filled.

words.meaning: The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
words.breakdown: Repeating valence shell configurations produce repeating chemical behaviour.
words.trap: The law is about atomic number, not atomic mass. Mendeleev used mass and got argon and potassium out of order.

words.meaning: A horizontal row of the periodic table, with the same outermost shell number.
words.breakdown: The first three periods have 2, 8 and 8 elements; later periods have 18 and 32.
words.trap: Period number equals the highest principal quantum number, not the number of electrons.

words.meaning: A vertical column, whose members share valence shell configuration.
words.breakdown: Group 1 is the alkali metals, group 17 the halogens, group 18 the noble gases.
words.trap: Elements in the same group do not have identical properties. They share the number of valence electrons, and properties change gradually down the group.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><rect class='d-line' x='24' y='30' width='80' height='30'/><rect class='d-line' x='104' y='30' width='80' height='30'/><rect class='d-line' x='184' y='30' width='80' height='30'/><rect class='d-muted' x='24' y='60' width='240' height='24'/><rect class='d-line' x='24' y='84' width='240' height='24'/><text class='d-label' x='30' y='50'>s block</text><text class='d-label' x='110' y='50'>p block</text><text class='d-label' x='190' y='50'>d block</text><text class='d-label' x='30' y='100'>f block</text><text class='d-label' x='30' y='132'>blocks follow the subshell being filled</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A schematic table divided into s, p, d and f blocks, labelled by the subshell being filled.
paragraphs.hook: The periodic table is not a list of elements. It is a picture of electron configurations.
paragraphs.exam_note: Questions ask the block, group or period of an element from its configuration. The highest n gives the period, and the valence subshell gives the block.
paragraphs.trap: Helium is in group 18 with the noble gases, but its configuration is 1s², so it belongs to the s block, not the p block.

recall.q: The modern periodic law arranges elements by
recall.why: Ordering by atomic number fixed the inversions that Mendeleev's mass ordering could not explain.

recall.q: An element with configuration 3s²3p⁵ belongs to
recall.why: Seven valence electrons place it in group 17, and the last electron enters a p orbital, so it is in the p block.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the group numbering used in your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: atomic and ionic radii
paragraphs.meaning: Atomic radius falls across a period because the nuclear charge grows while electrons enter the same shell, pulling them closer. It rises down a group because each new shell starts further out. Ions follow the same logic: a cation is smaller than its atom and an anion is larger, since losing electrons raises the effective pull on those that remain.

words.meaning: A measure of the size of an atom, defined by the distance between nuclei in a bonded or touching pair.
words.breakdown: Covalent, metallic and van der Waals radii are defined differently and give different numbers.
words.trap: There is no single atomic radius. Comparing values from different definitions gives false trends.

words.meaning: The net positive charge felt by an outer electron after inner electrons shield part of the nucleus.
words.breakdown: It rises across a period, which is why radius falls.
words.trap: Effective nuclear charge is not the same as the actual nuclear charge. The inner electrons screen part of it.

words.meaning: Ions or atoms with the same number of electrons.
words.breakdown: Among isoelectronic species, the one with the larger nuclear charge is smaller.
words.trap: Isoelectronic species do not have the same radius. Na+ is smaller than F- because sodium has the higher nuclear charge.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 118h260M30 118V30'/><path class='d-accent' d='M36 44c60 0 90 26 120 40 40 18 90 24 128 26'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='64' cy='52' r='4'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='238' cy='88' r='4'/><text class='d-label' x='40' y='40'>Li, large</text><text class='d-label' x='176' y='116'>F, small</text><text class='d-label' x='30' y='140'>radius across period 2</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A curve falling across a period, showing atomic radius decreasing from lithium to fluorine.
paragraphs.hook: Adding electrons usually makes an atom bigger. Losing them always makes it smaller.
paragraphs.exam_note: Ranking questions are common: order a set of atoms or ions by size. Cations first, then isoelectronic comparisons by nuclear charge.
paragraphs.trap: A noble gas radius from van der Waals data looks larger than the halogen before it. That does not break the trend, because the measurement is a different kind.

recall.q: Which is larger, Na or Na+?
recall.why: Removing an electron leaves the same nuclear charge pulling fewer electrons, and often removes a whole shell, so the ion is smaller.

recall.q: Among Na+, Mg2+, F- and O2-, the smallest is
recall.why: All four are isoelectronic with ten electrons, and magnesium has the largest nuclear charge, so it pulls them in tightest.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the radius data against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: ionisation enthalpy
paragraphs.meaning: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from a gaseous atom. It rises across a period as the outer electron is held more tightly, and falls down a group as the electron sits further from the nucleus. The trend is not smooth: beryllium holds its electron more tightly than boron, and nitrogen more tightly than oxygen, because of filled and half-filled subshells.

words.meaning: The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
words.breakdown: The first value removes the outermost electron; the second removes the next, and is always larger.
words.trap: The sample must be gaseous. Values measured in a liquid or solid include other energy changes and are not ionisation enthalpies.

words.meaning: The extra stability of a subshell that is exactly half full.
words.breakdown: Nitrogen has three unpaired 2p electrons, so its first ionisation enthalpy exceeds that of oxygen.
words.trap: Half-filled stability is a small effect, not a rule that overrides every trend. It explains exceptions, not the general direction.

words.meaning: The enthalpy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.
words.breakdown: It is usually negative, since energy is released, and chlorine releases more than fluorine.
words.trap: A more negative electron gain enthalpy does not always follow the group trend. Fluorine is smaller than chlorine, and adding an electron to it costs more repulsion.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 118h260M30 118V30'/><path class='d-accent' d='M36 108c40-8 60-24 80-28 30-6 40 10 70-6 30-16 50-30 90-44'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='116' cy='80' r='4'/><text class='d-label' x='112' y='66'>dip at boron</text><text class='d-label' x='166' y='92'>dip at oxygen</text><text class='d-label' x='30' y='140'>first ionisation enthalpy across period 2</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: An ionisation enthalpy curve rising across period 2 with two small dips at boron and oxygen.
paragraphs.hook: The trend is a staircase with two steps backwards, and those steps are the exam question.
paragraphs.exam_note: The classic exceptions are Be greater than B, and N greater than O. The reasons are a filled 2s subshell and a half-filled 2p subshell.
paragraphs.trap: Second ionisation enthalpy is always larger than the first for the same element, because the remaining electrons are held more tightly.

recall.q: The first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen is greater than that of oxygen because
recall.why: The half-filled 2p arrangement is relatively stable, so removing an electron from nitrogen costs more than removing one from oxygen.

recall.q: Ionisation enthalpy generally decreases down a group because
options: The outer electron is further from the nucleus
recall.why: Each period adds a shell, so the outer electron is more shielded and further away, and is easier to remove.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Classification of Elements and Periodicity: electronegativity and anomalies
paragraphs.meaning: Electronegativity is an atom's tendency in a bond to attract the shared electrons, and it rises across a period and falls down a group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element. Some apparent breaks in periodic trends are not breaks at all but consequences of a different measurement, such as the large van der Waals radius reported for noble gases.

words.meaning: The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract a shared pair of electrons.
words.breakdown: On the Pauling scale fluorine is 4.0, the highest value.
words.trap: Electronegativity has no unit and is not measured for a free atom. It only has meaning inside a bond.

words.meaning: The gradual decrease in size across the lanthanoids, caused by poor shielding of f electrons.
words.breakdown: It makes the elements after the lanthanoids slightly smaller than expected.
words.trap: The contraction is small but cumulative, which is why zirconium and hafnium have almost identical radii.

words.meaning: A radius that appears out of trend because a different definition was used.
words.breakdown: Noble gas radii are van der Waals radii, which are larger than covalent radii.
words.trap: The noble gas values are not evidence against the periodic trend. Comparing them with covalent radii is comparing two different quantities.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M24 116h272M24 116V30'/><path class='d-accent' d='M40 110c30-4 50-20 70-40 20-22 36-40 60-52'/><text class='d-label' x='36' y='140'>across a period: increases</text><text class='d-label' x='212' y='44'>F is the highest</text><path class='d-guide' d='M170 40v70'/><text class='d-label' x='176' y='92'>down a group: decreases</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A curve rising across a period to fluorine as the most electronegative element, with a note that it falls down a group.
paragraphs.hook: The noble gases look huge on a radius chart only because their radius is measured differently.
paragraphs.exam_note: Questions pair electronegativity with bond polarity and oxidation state. A larger difference means a more polar bond, not necessarily a stronger one.
paragraphs.trap: Electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy both measure attraction for electrons, but one is in a bond and the other is for an isolated gaseous atom.

recall.why: Fluorine has the highest value on the Pauling scale, at 4.0, because of its small size and high nuclear charge.

recall.q: The very large radius reported for neon is best explained by
options: A real break in the trend
The use of van der Waals radii
recall.why: Noble gases do not form covalent bonds, so their size is measured from van der Waals contact, a different and larger quantity.
